newsitem.title: USA: WJC considers probe of more neutral countries in war.
newsitem.headline: WJC considers probe of more neutral countries in war.

text.p: The World Jewish Congress, whose research into Switzerland's relations with the Nazis led to a major controversy in that country, is turning its attention to the actions of Europe's other neutral countries during the Second World War.

A WJC spokesman said on Friday the group's European chapters will meet on Sunday in Berlin for two days to discuss what its researchers have discovered so far on Spain, Portugal, Sweden and Turkey's dealings with the Third Reich and how its investigation should proceed.
WJC revelations about Switzerland's wartime financial relations with Switzerland led to an agonizing debate over whether that country profited from the Holocaust.
On Wednesday, the Swiss government announced a plan to create a huge humanitarian foundation to benefit victims of genocide, human rights abuses and natural disasters.

Most Swiss commentators praised the human rights foundation as a return to the moral high ground after months of battering on the world stage from critics who claimed Switzerland, which started the war afraid of a German invasion, became Hitler's money-launderers.

A WJC spokesman said the meeting, which will be attended by the heads of Jewish communities in 24 countries, will present a series of documents found in the U.S. National Archives that raise questions about whether the other neutral countries abused their neutrality, especially in their handling of gold looted by the Nazis.
"With the announcement of the humanitarian fund in Switzerland, we are shifting our resources to other European countries," WJC Executive director Elan Steinberg said.

Among documents the WJC have uncovered are a U.S. government report in 1945 stating that Portugal began the war with 116,800 lb (53,000 kilograms) of gold and ended it with 784,800 lb (356,000 kilograms) as it became a major depository, after Switzerland, for looted Nazi gold.
"It is clear that we are talking about billions of dollars in transferred assets just in the case of looted Nazi gold," Steinberg said.

He said several documents reveal that Hermann Goering, one of Hitler's chief henchmen, sent more than 200 stolen paintings to Spain for safekeeping and that his sister-in-law was active in buying property in Sweden.

Another document alleged that Turkey was in possession of 1,754 gold bars that had been stolen by the Nazis from Belgium and had melted them down and recast with the year 1937 stamped on them to avoid detection.
